beads.title: An --exit-node value is never resolved, so all six of Go's refusals are missing
beads.description: Go resolves the `--exit-node` argument in the CLI, against the status it has just fetched, before any pref is written. `Prefs.SetExitNodeIP` (ipn/prefs.go) refuses outright if `ExitNodeID` is already set (`ErrExitNodeIDAlreadySet`) and otherwise hands the string to `exitNodeIPOfArg`, which is six refusals in one function: a value that parses as an IP but belongs to this machine is `ExitNodeLocalIPError` ("cannot use %s as an exit node as it is a local IP address to this machine"), which both `up` and `set` re-wrap as "%w; did you mean --advertise-exit-node?"; once `BackendState == "Running"` an IP with no peer behind it is "no node found in netmap with IP %v" and a peer that is not offering exit is "node %v is not advertising an exit node"; a non-IP argument is matched against every peer in three spellings (base name, FQDN, FQDN sans trailing dot) and yields "cannot resolve exit node by hostname while Tailscale is starting up; please use its Tailscale IP address instead" when there are no peers yet, "invalid value %q for --exit-node; must be IP or peer hostname" on no match, and "ambiguous exit node name %q" on more than one. This fork checks exactly one thing. `validate_exit_node_selector` (src/ipn/mod.rs) rejects an `auto:` prefix and returns Ok for everything else, which then becomes a `tailscale::ExitNodeSelector` (a bare IP parses as `Ip`, anything else as `Name`) and goes to the engine unexamined — the same infallible-parse trap the `auto:` guard was written to close, left open for every other value. So `tnet up --exit-node 100.64.0.7` naming this node's own address, a mistyped peer name, or a peer that never advertised an exit node are all accepted, and the operator learns nothing: traffic is not routed and no command said why. The inputs are already here — `PeerReport.is_exit_node` (src/localapi.rs) carries the advertisement, `exit-node list` already builds its table from it, and `status` carries this node's own addresses. Decide where the resolution runs. Go does it CLI-side because that is where the status round-trip is; `Backend::check_prefs` (src/ipn/mod.rs) is the daemon-side alternative and has the advantage that `up`, `set` and the `check-prefs` verb share one implementation. Decide also to port Go's staging rather than a stricter rule: the local-IP and syntax refusals apply always, but the netmap-backed checks apply only once the node is Running, and hostname resolution is refused rather than attempted while the peer list is empty.

beads.title: --hostname takes any string, where Go rejects one that is not a valid DNS name
beads.description: `prefsFromUpArgs` (cmd/tailscale/cli/up.go) validates the hostname before it builds the prefs: `if err := dnsname.ValidHostname(upArgs.hostname); upArgs.hostname != "" && err != nil { return nil, err }`. `ValidHostname` (util/dnsname/dnsname.go) runs the name through `ToFQDN`, which refuses anything longer than 254 bytes, and then `ValidLabel` on every dot-separated label: not empty, at most 63 bytes, first and last byte alphanumeric, and every interior byte a letter, digit or `-`. The errors are `vizerror`s, so they are written to be shown to the person who typed the flag ("empty DNS label", "%q is not a valid DNS label: contains invalid character %q"). The check matters because the hostname is not local decoration: it becomes this node's MagicDNS name, so a rejected name is the difference between a failure at the moment of typing and a node that registers under a name nobody can resolve. This fork has no equivalent anywhere. `tnet up --hostname` and `tnet set --hostname` (src/bin/tnet.rs) carry an `Option<String>` straight through to the daemon, `Backend`'s prefs path stores it, and `src/ipn/config.rs` threads it into the engine `Config` — nothing between the flag and the wire looks at the bytes, so `tnet set --hostname "my laptop"`, `--hostname -leading-dash`, `--hostname a..b` and a 300-character name are all accepted. Note that upstream keeps one hostname rule in the daemon too: `checkPrefsLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) refuses the literal `badhostname.tailscale.`, deliberately kept "just for testing" — that one is a test hook, not a rule worth porting. The decision is the usual boundary question and it has a clear answer here: Go validates in the CLI, but this fork's `--config` loader (src/conffile.rs) can set the hostname without the CLI ever running, so the check belongs in the daemon's prefs validation where both paths reach it, with `tnet` free to fail earlier for a better message. Port the label rules as Go states them rather than an approximation — the 63-byte label and 254-byte name limits included — and port the empty case: an empty `--hostname` is not an error in Go, it means "unset".

beads.title: Funnel can be turned on while shields-up is set, which Go refuses in SetServeConfig
beads.description: The shields-up/Funnel exclusion is enforced on BOTH sides upstream, and this fork has neither. The prefs side is `checkFunnelEnabledLocked`; the serve side is the first thing `setServeConfigLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/serve.go) does: `if config.IsFunnelOn() && prefs.ShieldsUp() { return errors.New("Unable to turn on Funnel while shields-up is enabled") }`. Two rules, two messages, two entry points, one invariant — a node that both blocks incoming connections and publishes a public endpoint accepts nothing on that endpoint, and neither command's output shows it. This corrects an assumption recorded with the prefs-side gap, which reasoned that "Go re-checks nothing, so a node can still reach the bad state by enabling Funnel after shields-up": Go does re-check, here, and the faithful port is both halves. This fork's `Backend::set_serve_config` (src/ipn/mod.rs) is the counterpart of `SetServeConfig` and validates nothing about prefs — it warns when a funnel-enabled port forwards to a non-loopback backend, then persists and re-arms. Both inputs are in hand at that call site: `self.prefs.shields_up` (src/prefs.rs) and `serve::funnel_ports` (src/ipn/serve.rs), which returns the ports Funnel is armed on and is the exact analogue of Go's `IsFunnelOn`. So this is one guard at the top of one function, with Go's message. Decide the scope, because the fork's serve config reaches the daemon by more than one road: the `set-serve-config` LocalAPI verb, `tnet funnel`, and the foreground serve path that restores a previous config on exit. Go puts the check below all of them, in the single locked setter, and the restore path argues for the same choice here — a restore that re-arms Funnel under shields-up should fail the same way a fresh `funnel` would. Decide also whether the refusal survives the ordering Go leaves open: with the prefs-side rule ported too, neither order reaches the bad state, and the pair should be tested as a pair.

beads.title: A second serve on a busy port silently replaces the first instead of being refused
beads.description: `validateServeConfigUpdate` (ipn/ipnlocal/serve.go) compares the incoming serve config against the existing one and refuses conflicts, with a comment stating outright that its messages are shown to CLI users and must be diagnosable. The rule that applies to every deployment is the serve-type one: for each port in the incoming config that already exists, `serveTypeFromPortHandler` classifies both, and a change is refused with "want to serve %q, but port %d is already serving %q". Two more guard foreground sessions ("listener already exists for port %d" for a new foreground session landing on a busy port, "foreground listener already exists for port %d" for a background config overwriting a foreground one), and Services get the same serve-type rule with the service name appended. This fork writes the port map with a plain map insert (`ServeConfig.tcp` and `.web` are `BTreeMap`s in src/localapi.rs, and src/bin/tnet.rs inserts into them at every serve and funnel call site), so `tnet serve --tcp 443 tcp://localhost:8000` on a port already terminating HTTPS replaces the handler, reports success, and the previous serve is gone with no diagnostic — the operator finds out when the old backend stops receiving traffic. Nothing in `Backend::set_serve_config` (src/ipn/mod.rs) compares old against new. Port the serve-type rule and give it the existing config to compare against, which the daemon already loads. Two decisions. First, how much of the function to port: this fork has no foreground sessions in the daemon (a foreground serve is torn down by `tnet` itself, a deviation the ledger records) and its Services support is read-only, so the two foreground rules and the per-service rule have no state to run against today — say so rather than porting dead code, and leave the shape so they can be added when the daemon owns sessions. Second, the classifier: Go's `serveTypeFromPortHandler` is what decides two handlers are "the same kind", and this fork's `TcpPortHandler`/`HttpHandler` split is not field-for-field Go's, so the port needs its own honest mapping of handler shape to serve type rather than a copy.

beads.title: set --auto-update is accepted on an installation that can never apply an update
beads.description: `checkAutoUpdatePrefsLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) is the fifth child of `checkPrefsLocked` and refuses an auto-update opt-in the node cannot honour: "Auto-update support is disabled in this build" when the build lacks the client-update feature, and "Auto-updates are not supported on this platform." when `feature.CanAutoUpdate()` is false. Both fire only on `Apply.EqualBool(true)` — declining or never stating is always legal — and because the check sits in the shared chain it guards `up`, `set` and any LocalAPI prefs edit. The rule exists because `AutoUpdate.Apply` is not a local preference: it is advertised to control as `Hostinfo.AllowsUpdate`, so a node that sets it is telling the tailnet admin that a remote update trigger will be honoured. Letting a node claim that when it has no updater is how an admin ends up believing a fleet is patched. This fork accepts the claim unconditionally. `--auto-update`/`--no-auto-update` are registered on `set` (src/bin/tnet.rs), `Prefs::auto_update_apply` (src/prefs.rs) is the tri-state mirror of Go's `opt.Bool`, and `src/ipn/config.rs` threads it to the engine, which sets `Hostinfo.AllowsUpdate` on registration and on every map request. `Backend::check_prefs` (src/ipn/mod.rs) does not look at it. And this fork already computes Go's predicate, twice, in the one place it matters: the install path of `run_update` (src/bin/tnet.rs) refuses `--yes` when `running_binary_homebrew_formula` says a package manager owns the binary ("use `brew upgrade`"), and refuses again when `host_release_triple` finds no published artifact for the host — this project ships Linux x86_64/aarch64 tarballs only, so on macOS, which this daemon builds and runs on, the binary provably cannot replace itself. That pair of refusals IS `CanAutoUpdate`; it is simply never consulted when the pref is set. Decide the predicate before porting the refusal, because it is the whole content of this bead. The honest reading is that this daemon has no background updater at all — `tnet update` is operator-invoked, as `Prefs::auto_update_apply`'s own rustdoc states — so a literal port would refuse the flag everywhere and delete a pref this fork deliberately carries. The narrow reading is to lift the two conditions `run_update` already applies and refuse only where the binary provably cannot replace itself; the widest is to keep accepting the pref and make the advertisement honest some other way. Whichever is taken, record it where the pref is documented, because today the rustdoc and the flag disagree about what setting it means.

beads.title: There is no control-to-node channel, so control can ask this node for nothing
beads.description: Upstream has a whole RPC surface this ledger has never carried a row for. `ipn/ipnlocal/c2n.go` implements a small HTTP server the control plane reaches over the existing noise session: `RegisterC2N` maps method+path patterns to handlers, `handleC2N` dispatches, and the registrations are spread across the tree — `/echo`, `POST /logtail/flush`, `POST /sockstats`, the `/debug/*` family (prefs, metrics, netmap, health, goroutines, component-logging, pprof), `POST /netfilter-kind`, plus `GET`+`POST /update` (feature/clientupdate/clientupdate.go), `GET /posture/identity` (feature/posture/posture.go), `GET /appconnector/routes` (feature/appconnectors/appconnectors.go), `POST /wol` (feature/wakeonlan/wakeonlan.go), `GET /vip-services` (ipn/ipnlocal/serve.go), `GET /tls-cert-status` (ipn/ipnlocal/cert.go) and `/ssh/usernames` (ssh/tailssh/tailssh.go). This is the mechanism by which an admin console acts on a node rather than merely reading about it. Its absence here is already visible in the fork's own documentation without being named: `Prefs::posture_checking` (src/prefs.rs) records that posture is "a c2n pull" nothing answers, so the pref's on-the-wire behaviour is byte-for-byte the disabled case; `Prefs::auto_update_apply` records that the node advertises `Hostinfo.AllowsUpdate` while "nothing here acts on a trigger"; and the app-connector route readback filed as engine ask #39 is the LocalAPI half of a readback control performs over `GET /appconnector/routes`. Three documented reductions, one missing mechanism. The work is to file it as an engine ask and give the ledger the row, not to build it: the c2n request arrives inside the control noise session, which the engine owns end to end, so the daemon cannot serve a handler the engine will not dispatch to it. Decide the shape of the ask, which is the substance. The minimum useful primitive is a registration hook — the engine surfaces the decoded request and takes the daemon's response — because that is what lets the daemon answer for state only it holds (prefs, serve config, posture). Decide also which handlers this fork would want first if the ask lands, and be selective in public: `/update` and `/posture/identity` are the two that make prefs this fork already carries mean something, while the `/debug/*` family is a remote read of daemon internals and deserves its own security judgement before anything answers it.

beads.title: The SSH-server gate is a build check only, missing Go's admin and platform refusals
beads.description: Go runs `featureknob.CanRunTailscaleSSH()` (envknob/featureknob/featureknob.go) from `checkSSHPrefsLocked` whenever `RunSSH` is being set, and it returns four distinct refusals: "The Tailscale SSH server does not run on Synology." and the same for QNAP (both liftable with the work-in-progress envknob), "The Tailscale SSH server does not run in sandboxed Tailscale GUI builds." on a sandboxed macOS build, "The Tailscale SSH server is not supported on " + the OS for anything outside linux/darwin/freebsd/openbsd/plan9, and — last, after the OS switch, so it applies everywhere — "The Tailscale SSH server has been administratively disabled." when `envknob.CanSSHD()` is false, which is `!Bool("TS_DISABLE_SSH_SERVER")`. That last one is the point of the function: it is how an operator or an image build turns the SSH server off for a machine regardless of what the tailnet or the user asks for, and it is portable — no distro detection, no GUI build, just an environment variable read at the moment the pref is checked. This fork's gate is the build feature and nothing else: `Backend::check_prefs` (src/ipn/mod.rs) refuses `ssh` when compiled without the `ssh` feature, with a message that names the Cargo feature, and its own comment scopes itself to "a faithful build-time check". So on an `ssh`-enabled build, `TS_DISABLE_SSH_SERVER=1 tnet set --ssh` starts the server. The fork already honours an envknob of exactly this shape elsewhere — `TS_DISABLE_PORTMAPPER` (src/portmap.rs) — so the precedent for reading one is set. Decide how much to port. `TS_DISABLE_SSH_SERVER` is the whole of the portable behaviour and should be read where the pref is checked, not where the server starts, so that `set --ssh` refuses rather than silently doing nothing. The unsupported-OS arm is a judgement call for a daemon that today builds for Linux and macOS: it can be ported as written, in which case it is dead on both, or declared covered by the build-feature gate — but say which. The Synology and QNAP arms need distro detection this fork has no other use for and should be declined explicitly rather than left unmentioned, which is what makes the next sweep stop re-finding them.
